title: Cost to Install HVAC in an Older Home
h1: How Much Does It Cost to Install HVAC in an Older Home?
description: Installing HVAC in an older home costs more or less depending on ductwork, electrical capacity, attic access and system type. Here is what drives the price.
quick_answer: There's no single price for putting HVAC in an older home. The cost depends on whether usable ductwork already exists, whether the electrical panel can handle a new system, how easy the attic is to work in, and whether you choose a ducted system, a heat pump or ductless mini-splits. A free in-home estimate is the only way to get a real number.
body:
Why do older homes cost more to fit with HVAC?

Newer houses are built with a spot for the furnace, a chase for the ducts and an electrical panel sized for central air. Many older San Diego homes were not. Some only had a wall furnace or a floor furnace, and some had nothing but a fireplace and open windows.

That means an installer may need to create space for equipment, run ductwork where none exists, and upgrade wiring before the new system can go in. Each of those steps adds labor and materials, which is why two homes with the same square footage can get very different quotes.

What changes the price the most?

These are the items we look at first when we walk an older home:

  • Existing ductwork. If the house has ducts in decent shape, they may be reused after cleaning and sealing. Old ducts that are crushed, disconnected or wrapped in failing insulation usually need to be replaced.
  • Attic access and clearance. Low-pitched roofs and tight attics slow the work down. Ducts and air handlers in Southern California homes often live in the attic, so access matters a lot.
  • Electrical capacity. Central air and heat pumps need dedicated circuits. An older panel may not have room, and a panel upgrade is work for a licensed electrician.
  • Gas line and venting. A new gas furnace needs a properly sized gas line and a vent that meets current code. Older flues sometimes don't.
  • System type and size. A heat pump, a gas furnace with AC, and ductless mini-splits all have different equipment and labor costs. Size should come from a load calculation, not a guess.
  • Permits and code updates. New installs need permits, and the inspector will expect current safety standards even if the rest of the house is decades old.

Ducted system or ductless mini-splits?

For a house with no ducts at all, ductless mini-splits are often the simpler path. Each indoor head is connected to an outdoor unit through a small line set, so there's no need to cut big runs through walls and ceilings. They also let you heat and cool only the rooms you use.

If the home already has ducts, or has a roomy attic where ducts can be run cleanly, a central heat pump or furnace and AC combination usually makes more sense. It keeps the indoor walls clear and handles the whole house from one thermostat. Some older homes end up with a mix: central air for the main living area and a mini-split for an add-on room or converted garage.

What else should you plan for in an older house?

A new system can only do so much if the house leaks air everywhere. Before or during the install, it's worth checking a few things:

  • Attic insulation that has settled, gone missing or been damaged by rodents
  • Gaps around old windows, can lights and attic hatches
  • Asbestos-wrapped duct joints or old duct tape on very old systems, which need proper handling before removal
  • Hall closet or garage furnace locations that may need a larger platform or better combustion air

Fixing insulation and air leaks can let you go with a smaller system that runs more evenly. Inland homes that see hot summers benefit the most, but coastal homes notice the difference on cold nights too.

How do you get an accurate number?

Ask for an in-home visit rather than a phone quote. A good estimate should include a load calculation, a look at the attic and ducts, a check of the electrical panel, and a written scope that lists equipment, ductwork, permits and cleanup. If a quote doesn't mention the ducts at all in an older home, ask why.

Our team handles new installs and replacements across San Diego County and Orange County. You can read more about our HVAC installation and replacement service, or check the current specials before you book your free estimate.

Is it worth adding HVAC to an older home?

For most owners, yes. Inland neighborhoods get hot enough in summer that central cooling makes the house far more livable, and even near the coast a quiet, efficient heat source beats a wall heater on a cold January night. Wildfire smoke days are another reason: a ducted system with a good filter lets you keep windows shut and still move clean air through the house.

The key is matching the system to the house. A heat pump sized correctly for a well-sealed 1960s ranch home will be more comfortable and cheaper to run than an oversized unit pushed through leaky old ducts.
faqs: Can I reuse the old ductwork in an older home?

Sometimes. If the ducts are intact, properly sized and can be sealed and cleaned, reusing them saves money. Ducts that are crushed, torn, poorly insulated or badly undersized usually cost you more in lost air than replacing them would.
Do I need a permit to install HVAC in an older house?

Yes. New HVAC installations and replacements need a permit, and the inspection checks things like gas lines, venting, electrical connections and refrigerant work. A contractor should pull the permit as part of the job.
Is a heat pump a good choice for an older San Diego home?

Often it is. Heat pumps handle both heating and cooling, and our mild winters suit them well. The house may need an electrical upgrade, and the attic insulation should be checked so the system isn't fighting heat loss.
How long does an HVAC install take in an older home?
A straight replacement can be done in a day or two. A new install with ductwork, electrical upgrades or mini-splits in several rooms takes longer. Your estimate should give a realistic schedule.
